title: Waves
seo_title: Waves Class 11 Physics Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 14)
standard_text: Wave motion, transverse and longitudinal waves, speed of travelling wave, displacement relation for a progressive wave, principle of superposition of waves, reflection of waves, standing waves in strings and organ pipes, fundamental mode and harmonics, beats.
meta_desc: Free CBSE Class 11 Physics worksheets for NCERT Chapter 14 Waves: transverse and longitudinal waves, v = fλ, wave speed on a string, sound in air, standing waves in strings and pipes, and beats. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: v = fλ; on a string v = √(T/μ).
key_sub: Open pipe f = v/2L; closed pipe f = v/4L (odd harmonics only).
body_html:
How to think about it

A wave carries energy without carrying matter. In transverse waves (strings) particles move at right angles to the wave; in longitudinal waves (sound) they move along it. For every wave v = fλ; on a string v = √(T/μ), and sound in air speeds up as √T.

Waves superpose. Reflected waves form standing waves with nodes λ/2 apart. A string or open pipe has all harmonics f = nv/2L; a pipe closed at one end has only odd harmonics f = nv/4L. Two close frequencies give beats at |f₁ − f₂| per second.

Example

Closed pipe 0.85 m, v = 340 m/s?

340 ÷ (4 × 0.85)

Answer: 100 Hz

Example

256 Hz and 260 Hz together?

260 − 256

Answer: 4 beats/s

Common mistakes

  • Using v/2L for a closed pipe.
  • Thinking sound travels in a vacuum.
  • Thinking a closed pipe has even harmonics.

faq.a: Periodic changes in loudness when two sounds of slightly different frequency are heard together; the beat frequency is |f₁ − f₂|.

faq.q: Why does a closed pipe give only odd harmonics?
faq.a: Its closed end must be a node and the open end an antinode, so L = λ/4, 3λ/4, 5λ/4, …

items.q: What are beats?
c: regular rise and fall of loudness when two close frequencies are heard together
